GROK Bot / Yes — the photo is a Pavestone Holland 7.75 in. × 4 in. × 1.75 in. (≈45 mm) Charcoal Concrete Paver (model #22003).

It’s the thinner Holland-style rectangular concrete paver (textured charcoal/gray surface), typically sold by the full pallet (672 pieces / ~145 sq ft). It’s intended mainly for patios, walkways, and lighter traffic rather than heavy vehicle use.
Where to get it (or close matches)

Home Depot — The exact pallet version is listed (model 22003):
 Pavestone Holland 45 mm Charcoal Concrete Paver (672-piece / 145 sq ft pallet)
Recent pricing has been in the ~$1,520–$1,570 range per pallet. Availability varies by location (ship-to-store or delivery options are common; local stock is often limited, which matches the original poster’s experience).
Super Arbor and similar online hardscape sellers also list the same or nearly identical 45 mm charcoal Holland pallet with delivery to the contiguous U.S.
SiteOne Landscape Supply — Carries Keystone (related brand) Holland Stone in charcoal in both 45 mm and the more common 60 mm thicknesses. Branches can special-order; check a local branch for stock/substitutes.
Texas-specific options (relevant since the poster is MaryTilesTexas):
Outdoor Warehouse Supply (Dallas/Plano area) is a Pavestone/Keystone master distributor. They stock Holland Stone pavers (including charcoal) and offer statewide Texas delivery. Contact them for current charcoal inventory — they primarily carry the thicker 60 mm versions but can source related products.
Similar alternatives if the exact thin charcoal is out of stock
Thicker 60 mm Pavestone/Keystone/Belgard Holland in charcoal (more durable, better for light vehicle traffic; ~103 sq ft per pallet). Widely available at landscape suppliers and some Home Depot locations.
Oldcastle or other brands’ 4×8 Holland-style charcoal/gray concrete pavers (Home Depot often has the 1.75 in. Oldcastle version).

Other dark gray / charcoal rectangular pavers in the same nominal size from Belgard, Unilock, or local manufacturers.

text:
The bipartisan House Select Committee report, Rigging the Game, reads less like an objective economic diagnosis and more like a convenient exercise in political deflection. By framing American deindustrialization strictly as the outcome of a nefarious Beijing plot—"predatory trade practices" and state-directed planning—Washington absolves itself of the structural choices it made over the past four decades.

Nobody "stole" America’s industrial base under cover of darkness. American corporations and policymakers actively dismantled it in pursuit of financialized, short-term shareholder returns, and the underlying mechanics of the global monetary system locked that trajectory in place.

1. The Triffin Dilemma: Why Imports Always Beat Domestic Production

To understand why importing from China—or anywhere else—became systematically cheaper than manufacturing in the United States, one need not look to Zhongnanhai. One need only look at the Triffin Dilemma, the foundational contradiction of the post-Bretton Woods monetary order.

Because the U.S. dollar serves as the world’s primary reserve and trade settlement currency, the United States must continuously supply the global economy with dollars to grease international commerce and meet foreign reserve demand. The only mechanism to pump those dollars outward at scale is for America to run persistent, structural current account and trade deficits.

This creates an inescapable structural bind:

An Artificially Strong Dollar: Relentless global demand for dollar-denominated assets keeps the U.S. dollar structurally overvalued relative to the currencies of manufacturing nations. An overvalued dollar acts as an automatic subsidy on imports and an automatic tax on American exports.
The Financialization Trade-Off: Capital naturally flows where returns are highest. In a reserve-currency economy, Wall Street and financial engineering yield far higher, faster returns than capital-intensive, low-margin industrial production. American boardrooms offshored factories not because they were tricked by Beijing, but because offshoring boosted quarterly earnings per share while Wall Street rewarded asset-light business models.

Washington wants to have its cake and eat it too: it demands the "exorbitant privilege" of issuing the world's reserve currency—allowing it to fund massive fiscal deficits and project global power on credit—without accepting the inevitable corollary: the hollowing out of its domestic manufacturing base. You cannot be both the world's supreme financial empire and its workshop.

2. Misreading China’s Industrial Ecosystem

The report reduces China’s manufacturing ascent to a caricature of top-down state subsidies and "whole-of-society" coercion. While Beijing undoubtedly deploys strategic industrial policy—just as the U.S. did during the 19th century and throughout the Cold War—subsidies alone do not build world-leading supply chains. If throwing money at a sector guaranteed dominance, Washington’s recent multi-billion-dollar outlays would have already solved its semiconductor and shipbuilding deficits.

What the Select Committee ignores is ecosystem density and agglomeration economics. Over thirty years, China built deep, hyper-competitive domestic supply chains, world-class logistics infrastructure, and an immense pool of vocational and engineering talent. In sectors like mature-node semiconductors or machine tools, Chinese firms succeeded not merely because of state procurement, but because hyper-intense domestic competition forced rapid iteration, cost discipline, and localized supply integration that fragmented Western firms could no longer match.

3. The Illusion of "Manhattan Project" Reindustrialization

Calling for a "Manhattan Project" to rebuild American manufacturing ignores why Western capital refuses to invest in domestic capacity today. Reindustrialization requires patient capital, reliable energy infrastructure, a deep vocational workforce, and predictable policy. Instead, Washington offers erratic tariffs, export controls that cut U.S. firms off from their largest revenue markets, and political theater.

Until Washington confronts the structural reality of the Triffin Dilemma and its own addiction to financialized capitalism, no amount of blaming Beijing will make manufacturing in Ohio cheaper than importing from Guangdong.

text:
From Grok.

Federal Examples
Emergency Medicaid: Federal law requires coverage of emergency medical conditions (including labor/delivery and certain prenatal/postpartum care) for those who meet income rules but lack qualifying status. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated more than $16.2 billion in federal and state spending on these services for illegal aliens since Biden took office, a roughly 124% increase versus the prior comparable period.⁠https://t.co/3tQ62p66R8
FEMA Shelter and Services Program (SSP) and predecessor Emergency Food and Shelter Program-Humanitarian: Congress appropriated hundreds of millions annually (e.g., ~$800 million in FY2023 and $650 million in FY2024) from Customs and Border Protection funds, administered by FEMA, for shelter, food, transportation, acute medical care, and related services for noncitizen migrants released from DHS custody. Cumulative funding for these migrant-specific programs exceeded $1.5 billion since 2021. Grants went to cities (including large ones to New York City) and NGOs. These are separate from FEMA’s Disaster Relief Fund.⁠Americanimmigrationcouncil
HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement and related spending: Watchdog analyses reported roughly $22.6 billion in HHS assistance from 2020–2024 tied to migrants, unaccompanied children, resettlement services, and expanded eligibility groups (including certain parolees). This includes care for unaccompanied minors and other supports.⁠Nationalreview
Mass parole programs creating “qualified alien” status: Biden expanded parole for Afghans, Ukrainians (Uniting for Ukraine), and Cubans/Haitians/Nicaraguans/Venezuelans (CHNV process, hundreds of thousands). Parole of at least one year generally makes recipients “qualified aliens” eligible for certain federal benefits (e.g., SNAP, Medicaid/CHIP with waiting periods or specific exceptions; Afghans and Ukrainians received refugee-like benefits under legislation). Work authorization was also routinely granted. Purely undocumented people without such status remained restricted.⁠Congress
American Rescue Plan (2021) flexible funds used by states for cash aid: States directed hundreds of millions of ARPA dollars to undocumented residents excluded from federal stimulus. Examples include Washington’s ~$340 million program for $1,000 grants and substantial programs in Illinois, New York, and elsewhere.⁠Fox News
Tax credits and other: U.S.-born (citizen) children in mixed-status households access Child Tax Credit, EITC, SNAP, and other benefits, with estimated multi-billion-dollar annual costs. WIC nutrition benefits, public K-12 education (constitutionally required), immunizations, and limited emergency disaster aid are also available regardless of status. Direct federal healthcare-related grants aimed at serving this population totaled ~$197 million since FY2021 in one analysis.
State and Local Examples
California Medi-Cal expansion: The state uses its own general funds (not federal Medicaid match for full coverage) to provide full-scope Medi-Cal to income-eligible undocumented residents of all ages. Full adult expansion was completed in 2024. State estimates put the annual general-fund cost at roughly $8.5–9.5 billion (higher than budgeted; ~1.6 million enrolled), contributing to multi-billion-dollar program shortfalls.⁠Thecentersquare
New York City migrant sheltering: The city spent multiple billions of dollars (cumulative figures approaching or exceeding $10 billion through recent fiscal years, with peaks like ~$3.75 billion in one year) on hotels, shelters, food, and services for asylum seekers and recent arrivals, at per-household rates often cited around $350–$390 per day. Federal SSP grants and New York State reimbursements offset portions, but the city covered the majority. Similar pressures hit other cities.⁠https://t.co/MbgC2js3JO
Other state programs: At least a dozen states plus D.C. fund their own Medicaid-like coverage for some or all undocumented residents (often children or broader groups). Many states offer in-state college tuition and some financial aid regardless of status. Local governments provide shelter, food assistance, and other services, especially in sanctuary jurisdictions.

text:
HOME ALONE: 5 BEHIND-THE-SCENES STORIES YOU MAY NOT KNOW!

On November 16, 1990, Home Alone arrived in theaters. Thirty-six years later, Kevin McCallister is still part of Christmas in millions of homes.

But some of the stories behind the movie are almost as entertaining as the movie itself!

1. It started with a real family vacation.

While preparing for a family trip to Europe in 1989, writer John Hughes began wondering what would happen if a parent accidentally left a child behind. That little moment of travel anxiety eventually became Home Alone.

2. The first draft took just nine days!

After returning from vacation, Hughes wrote the screenplay in only nine days. According to his son James, the final 44 pages were written during one eight-hour marathon. Talk about working under pressure!

3. Chris Farley almost played Santa Claus.

Before becoming a household name on Saturday Night Live, Farley auditioned to play the Santa Kevin encounters. Director Chris Columbus later recalled that Farley apparently hadn't slept the night before. The audition didn't go well, and Ken Hudson Campbell got the part.

4. Mother Nature rewrote the snow budget.

The production hadn't originally planned for artificial snow. Then a blizzard arrived on the second day of filming! Suddenly, the filmmakers had to maintain a snowy Chicago winter throughout the movie, even after the real snow melted.

5. We can thank Chevy Chase for Chris Columbus directing the movie!

Columbus was originally supposed to direct National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation. But after clashing with Chevy Chase, he walked away. John Hughes later offered him Home Alone instead.

And just like that, one Christmas classic led to another.

6. Kevin's childhood home became a $5.5 million piece of movie history!

Remember that beautiful house where Kevin McCallister defended himself against the Wet Bandits?

The real house, located in Winnetka, Illinois, reportedly sold in January 2025 for a whopping $5.5 million!

That's quite a jump from its previous sale price of $1.585 million in 2012.

Apparently, being one of the most recognizable houses in Christmas movie history has its perks!

Which of these five stories surprised you the most?

text:
Nowhere on Earth produces more almonds than California.

The state supplies nearly 80% of the world's almonds. That's enough to fill 50,000 semi-trucks, bumper to bumper.

But almonds weren't always a California success story.

In the late 1700s, Spanish missionaries brought almonds to Mexico, then north into Alta California.

Along the coast, they built 21 missions, stretching from San Diego to Sonoma.

One of the most ambitious was Mission San Gabriel Arcángel, founded in 1771 near what's now Los Angeles. The missionaries planted citrus, olives, grapes, and almonds.

But the almond trees, likely early Spanish types like Desmayo Largueta, struggled.

The coastal humidity slowed their growth, and the harvests were sparse.

Meanwhile, other crops flourished.

Grapes became wine. Olives yielded oil. Citrus took over the inland valleys.

These Mediterranean staples helped shape California's early farming identity.

Almonds quietly vanished from the landscape.

For nearly a century, they were forgotten, until new settlers from the east arrived, bringing different crops, new methods, and a hunger for what California soil could offer.

Among them was a curious entrepreneur named Arthur T. Hatch.

Like many Californians at the time, he dabbled in mining, trade, and postal work before landing on farming.

On a hundred acres of land near Vacaville, he planted dozens of fruit and nut trees side by side, testing which could handle the region's heat and drought.

He watched which trees bloomed early, which nuts cracked cleanly, and, most importantly, which came back strong year after year.

One almond variety kept outperforming the rest.

Its kernels were large, sweet, and easy to shell. They required less labor and fetched higher prices when brought to the local market.

Hatch named it Nonpareil: "without equal."

In 1883, Hatch brought his products to the Vacaville Citrus Fair, a gathering that drew growers, nursery operators, and buyers from across California.

Most came expecting to see citrus, stone fruit, and grapes. Almonds were an outlier. Few believed they could be commercially grown here at all.

But Hatch's trees told a different story.

They had survived the Central Valley's climate. They had produced consistent, high-quality nuts. And now, they were on display for everyone to see.

The effect rippled.

Growers from other valleys saw the potential. Nurseries began requesting cuttings.

And for the first time, almonds were seen as a potential crop.

In a single season, Nonpareil went from curiosity to cornerstone.

Today, California almonds are everywhere.

Pressed into milk. Blended into protein bars. Ground into flour.

The edible kernel alone powers a multi-billion dollar global market.

But that's only part of the story.

Because the kernel, the part we eat, makes up just one-third of the almond by weight.

The other two-thirds?

They don't end up on your plate.

They're put to work in ways few consumers ever see.

text:
🧭 PRINCESS MARGARET BEACH | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Take a ferry from Kingstown, St. Vincent, to Port Elizabeth on Bequia (approximately one hour). From the harbour, follow the scenic Belmont Coastal Trail for a 20–25-minute walk to the beach. Water taxis offer an alternative across Admiralty Bay.

🏝️ What to Explore

Enjoy swimming in sheltered turquoise waters, admire yachts anchored offshore, or explore rocky sections near the shoreline for snorkelling. For a longer coastal outing, combine the beach with nearby Lower Bay and Port Elizabeth's waterfront.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow 2–4 hours for a relaxed beach visit, or half a day with lunch and coastal exploration. Day trips from St. Vincent are possible, provided ferry connections align.

🌤️ When to Visit

December–April generally offers drier weather and favourable conditions for outdoor activities. May–November is typically wetter, with fewer visitors.

💰 Costs & Planning

Beach access is free. Budget separately for ferries, water taxis, refreshments and optional beach facilities. Confirm transport fares, return schedules and service availability before travelling.

text:
"Solaris" (1972) A Journey into the Human Heart 

When Andrei Tarkovsky released "Solaris" in 1972, he redefined what a science fiction film could be. Instead of focusing on rockets and cosmic spectacle, he turned his camera inward, toward the landscape of the human soul. The result was a film that dared to question whether man's true frontier was the universe or his own conscience. 

Based on the great novel by Polish writer Stanisław Lem, "Solaris" follows a small crew orbiting a living planet that reads human thoughts and brings them to life. The premise is simple, but Tarkovsky uses it as a framework for a profound meditation on guilt, love, and the need for redemption. The planet is not an enemy to be defeated but a mirror that forces man to face what he would rather forget.

At the height of the Cold War and the space race, "Solaris" offered a quiet rebuke to the machinery of progress. Tarkovsky's film asked not how far humanity could go, but whether it deserved to go any farther. Its slow pace and lingering imagery were deliberate acts of resistance against an age infatuated with speed and certainty. What he gave instead was a study of memory and mercy, played out among the stars. The journey outward became a journey home. 

Full movie review can be found here. https://t.co/6A3mmqjBT8

text:
Six days after JonBenét Ramsey (6) was found murdered in her family’s Boulder home, her parents sat down for a televised CNN interview.

But police were still trying to get them to sit down for formal questioning.

According to an April 23, 1997 statement from the Boulder Police Department, investigators had requested interviews immediately after JonBenét’s murder.

The department said the Ramseys declined to be formally interviewed before leaving Colorado for their daughter’s funeral.

Then came the January negotiations.

According to police, the Ramseys’ attorneys proposed that:

John and Patsy be interviewed together.
The interviews take place at their attorney’s office.
Patsy’s doctor be present.
Their attorneys choose which detectives could question them.
Patsy’s interview last no longer than one hour.

Police rejected those conditions.

The Ramsey attorneys disputed the department’s account, maintaining that their clients had offered to cooperate and that police had canceled scheduled interviews.

But the dates aren’t disputed.

January 1, 1997: John and Patsy appear on CNN.

April 30, 1997: Their first extensive formal police interviews finally take place.

125 days after their daughter was found murdered.

The parents had spoken with officers during the initial investigation. But speaking with officers at the scene is not the same as submitting to separate, detailed interviews about a child’s homicide.

And the investigators responsible for finding JonBenét’s killer had been trying to obtain those interviews for months.

Source: Boulder Police Department, April 23, 1997, Ramsey Case Update #41.

text:
Karla's trafficker crushed her ribs, starved her and kept her on meth so she'd hit a $2,500 a day quota, and when she finally escaped, she went back.

In rap videos she was the white girl with the guns and tattoos. After one shoot in Baton Rouge the rapper and three friends rode back to the room she rented and all wanted sex instead of paying her, so she said she needed to freshen up, walked straight out the back door and drove off. By the time she pulled over at a Walmart her phone was blowing up with threats and her car was full of their guns, drugs, jewelry and cash.

A friend hiding her said he knew someone who could help, a man she only ever knew as Fat. He treated her like a queen at first and took her places she'd wanted to see since she was a kid. Then he had her drive a young girl in a red wig to dates, and one night when the girl came back with no money he made Karla pull over near the swamps in Louisiana. She watched in the rear view mirror as he dragged the girl out and beat her, then he made her leave the girl on the side of the road. She never found out what happened to her.

Soon he had Karla on Backpage under a photo stolen from a porn site, with her first client at a casino. The quota started at $1,500 a day, and missing it meant beatings and being made to do things she'd never agree to, city after city from Baton Rouge through Texas to Colorado. At the top of Pikes Peak a woman offered to take their picture and he said he doesn't take pictures with hoes, which is when she understood he never loved her.

Back in Houston he left her keys on the dresser, and she ran down three flights of stairs in heels, under 100 pounds, and drove as far as she could, until messages threatening her family made her turn around. Her husband called the police, and Texas DPS opened a case.

Federal agents seized Backpage on April 6, 2018, after years of accusations that it was a hub for sex trafficking.

Karla: a woman who robbed the wrong rappers or proof that trafficking starts with someone treating you like a queen?

text:
**Roughly $1,700–$2,500 door-to-door from Miami (most realistic range for a Cybertruck in 2026), with port-to-port options potentially lower if you self-deliver.** Exact pricing requires a custom quote because the Cybertruck is oversized and an EV.

### Key Cost Drivers and Estimates

Standard sedans from Miami/Florida to San Juan typically run $1,200–$1,550 (door-to-door or near it). SUVs/trucks are higher, often $1,450–$1,850.

The Cybertruck is larger and heavier than typical pickups:

- Length: ~223.7 inches (18.6 ft)
- Width (mirrors folded): ~86.6 inches (exceeds many carriers’ 82-inch standard tiers)
- Height: ~70.5 inches
- Weight: ~6,600–6,900 lbs

This triggers oversize/weight surcharges (commonly $150–$350+ on domestic lanes) and limits trailer or vessel space, pushing it into custom-quote territory. Open RoRo is the most affordable method; enclosed/container is safer for the high value but costs more (often 30–50%+ higher).

Realistic all-in estimates (ocean + inland trucking from Miami area + fees):

- **Door-to-door (Miami pickup to San Juan area)**: $1,800–$2,500+
- **Port-to-port** (you drop at Jacksonville or similar; pick up in San Juan): Closer to $1,300–$1,800 base for oversized, plus any short trucking

Jacksonville (JAXPORT) is the main and usually cheapest gateway, with frequent sailings. Miami/Port Everglades options exist but are less frequent; most Florida shipments route via Jacksonville. Ocean transit is typically 2.5–7 days (TOTE ~55 hours; Crowley ~2.5 days); total door-to-door is often 7–14 days including processing.

### Carrier Notes (Important for Cybertruck/EV)

- **Crowley**: Primary viable option. Accepts EVs (typically requires 30–50% battery charge; no damaged/inoperable units). Offers below-deck enclosed garages for better protection. Handles oversized as breakbulk/custom.
- **TOTE Maritime**: Does **not** accept EVs or PHEVs (policy since ~Aug 2025 due to fire risk). Rates for standard vehicles ~$1,210–$1,310 from Jacksonville depending on dimensions.
- **Trailer Bridge**: Generally no longer accepting used EVs.

Book 2–3 weeks ahead, especially in peak seasons (holidays, summer). Multiple quotes from Crowley and experienced Puerto Rico brokers are essential.

### Extra Costs to Budget

- **Puerto Rico Hacienda excise tax (arbitrio)**: Currently **exempt for full EVs** (as of late 2026 info; confirm with Hacienda/SURI as rules can change). Gas vehicles face progressive rates that can be thousands on a high-value truck. No U.S. import duties/customs apply (Puerto Rico is a territory).
- Optional marine/cargo insurance (recommended for the value; often $25 per $1,000 of declared value or similar).
- Port fees, storage if delayed, destination handling, and PR registration/inspection (DTOP).
- Fuel limited to ~¼ tank for safety.

### Tips for the Best Price

1. Self-deliver to the Jacksonville terminal if practical (cheapest).
2. Compare Crowley direct vs. brokers (some specialize in this lane).
3. Choose RoRo over container unless you need max protection or are shipping non-running.
4. Prepare documents: title (or lienholder letter), registration, photo ID, insurance proof.
5. Document the vehicle thoroughly with photos/video before handover.
6. Confirm current EV battery and acceptance rules, as policies vary.

Get live quotes from Crowley and a couple of reputable auto transport brokers that regularly handle Florida–Puerto Rico and oversized/EV vehicles—prices fluctuate with fuel, demand, and space. Rates above are 2026 market estimates based on published carrier data and industry ranges for similar routes/vehicles.

text:
$NWBO #DCVax

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗜 𝗗𝗖𝗩𝗔𝗫 𝗣𝗟𝗔𝗡 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗡𝗘𝗘𝗗 𝗔 𝗦𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗜 𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗧𝗢 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗥𝗧.

That changes the order of investment.

Northwest could supply an authorized Saudi program from its existing British manufacturing operation while a regional partner establishes access and develops local production.

The company would bring the vaccine, clinical evidence, intellectual property and manufacturing expertise. The partner would bring regional execution and whatever financial commitments the definitive agreement secures.

That is the commercial inflection point to watch: whether assets Northwest has already developed can support international expansion without Northwest having to build and finance every part of it itself.

𝗦𝗣𝗜𝗠𝗔𝗖𝗢 𝗜𝗦 𝗔𝗟𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗬 𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚.

On November 16, Genetix announced that Saudi marketing applications for LYFGENIA and ZYNTEGLO are under SFDA review through SPIMACO.

Both are FDA-approved therapies made from patients’ own blood stem cells.

Genetix announced its SPIMACO agreement on June 23. Confirmation of Saudi review followed 146 days later. The submission dates are undisclosed, so that measures the interval between announcements rather than regulatory review time.

It nevertheless demonstrates execution.

SPIMACO is responsible for authorization and commercialization, with Saudi manufacturing planned. The same company signed Northwest’s August DCVax-L memorandum.

Its operating scale also matters: SAR 1.70 billion in reported 2025 revenue and SAR 184.4 million in net profit, up more than sevenfold. Its SPIMACO Bio subsidiary targets biological, gene and cell therapies.

Northwest’s prospective partner is already doing the regulatory and commercial work contemplated for other individualized cell products.

𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗔𝗚𝗥𝗘𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗔𝗗𝗗𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗧𝗦 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗕𝗟𝗘𝗠.

Northwest’s August 6 MOU proposes a commercial relationship. It is non-binding, with the following division of responsibilities contemplated:

• SPIMACO handles the Saudi application, marketing, sales and distribution.

• Northwest provides the scientific evidence, support and manufactured vaccine.

• Northwest retains its intellectual property.

• Revenue sharing is contemplated, with separate agreements for Saudi manufacturing and technology transfer.

Glioblastoma comes first. Other indications and Gulf territories can follow by mutual agreement.

Then came the regulator-to-regulator agreement.

On November 16, MHRA announced a memorandum with SFDA, signed by Lawrence Tallon and Hisham Aljadhey at the DIA–MHRA summit in London, with Anthony Harnden present.

Its scope expressly includes biologics and advanced therapies. Rare diseases are among its initial priorities.

The company agreement would organize production, payment and distribution. The regulatory agreement establishes a framework for cooperation, information exchange and shared expertise.

A British-manufactured, patient-specific therapy seeking Saudi access sits directly within the kinds of cross-border problems those arrangements are intended to address.

𝗦𝗣𝗜𝗠𝗔𝗖𝗢 𝗣𝗔𝗬𝗦 𝗙𝗢𝗥 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗨𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘.

Its other transactions show the commercial model.

Genetix receives technology-transfer payments and a double-digit royalty. Shilpa Biologicals’ agreement includes upfront payments, development and commercial milestones, and product-supply revenue, followed by phased localization.

Those terms belong to those companies. They show what can be negotiated.

For Northwest, the potential value extends beyond supplying individual doses. The ability to reproduce the manufacturing process in another country is itself an asset.

Saudi Arabia has a strong incentive to acquire that capability. King Faisal Specialist Hospital reported that local CAR-T production reduced treatment cost from roughly SAR 1.3 million to SAR 250,000 and manufacturing time from 28 days to 12–14.

Those are CAR-T figures. They explain the economic motivation behind the Kingdom’s investment in advanced manufacturing.

Its National Biotechnology Strategy targets regional leadership by 2030 and global leadership by 2040.

Northwest’s proposed sequence fits that ambition: supply first, then negotiate the transfer of production capability while retaining IP.

𝗦𝗔𝗪𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗡 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗕𝗔𝗦𝗘.

Sawston received its MHRA commercial manufacturing licence in March 2023. Northwest’s announcement described permissions to export cellular products and import cellular starting materials into Britain.

Northwest acquired Advent, Sawston’s operator, in October 2025. The manufacturing business is now inside Northwest; the building is leased.

An initial Saudi program could connect local collection and treatment to British production, subject to the required product, site, tissue-shipment and import permissions.

Northwest historically estimated capacity of approximately 450–500 patients annually in the first two suites, occupying about 4,400 square feet of an 88,345-square-foot building. That describes potential production capacity, rather than spare slots available for a Saudi program.

Expansion remains a separate issue. Grade C construction began in November 2025, followed by a disclosed pause while engineering continued. The second-quarter filing discussed additional tumor-lysate processing capacity before completion. The latest filing does not establish that the new suite is finished.

On October 26, Northwest announced expansion of its technical team supporting manufacturing scale-up and other priority operations, including restarting U.S. manufacturing.

The distinction is useful: an operating production base can support an initial plan while additional capacity is developed.

𝗥𝗘𝗚𝗨𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗬 𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪𝗟𝗘𝗗𝗚𝗘 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗩𝗘𝗟 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗠𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗦.

SFDA issued its NADR rare-disease framework on August 5. Northwest announced its MOU on August 6. The framework took effect September 5.

NADR covers qualifying pharmaceutical and biological products, including products still in development. Prior foreign approval is not universally required.

Its designation-assessment target is 20 working days from a complete submission, subject to information requests. A marketing application should follow within six months of designation.

The framework includes rolling submission, conditional approval and natural-history comparators where concurrent controls are infeasible.

For manufacturing sites in listed countries, including Britain, it provides inspection flexibility supported by GMP certificates, the site master file and inspection documentation.

Sawston already has a British regulatory record. Relevant existing documentation could support Saudi assessment without first relocating production.

NADR also permits established platform knowledge and related manufacturing data to support subsequent submissions.

That makes accumulated manufacturing knowledge potentially useful across both territories and future development programs. Each proposed indication still needs an adequate evidence case, but every part of the supporting work need not necessarily begin again.

Regulatory information exchange also remains separate from commercial technology transfer. Cooperation between agencies does not automatically license Northwest’s manufacturing process to another company.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗖𝗞𝗔𝗚𝗘 𝗔𝗟𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗗𝗬 𝗛𝗔𝗦 𝗦𝗨𝗕𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗡𝗖𝗘.

DCVax-L’s published externally controlled survival analysis reported:

• Newly diagnosed glioblastoma: median survival of 19.3 versus 16.5 months.

• Five-year survival: 13.0% versus 5.7%.

• Recurrent glioblastoma: median survival of 13.2 versus 7.8 months.

Subsequent patient-level matching analyses tested the survival finding using individual records from other trials.

SFDA would assess that package. The relevance of NADR is that it provides mechanisms for discussing evidence appropriate to rare diseases and difficult trial settings.

Britain recognized the product’s promise much earlier: DCVax-L received the first UK Promising Innovative Medicine designation in 2014.

𝗕𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗦𝗛 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗔𝗟 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗦𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗜 𝗢𝗣𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦.

Some Saudi routes can be pursued beforehand.

The Breakthrough Medicine Program requires that a product has no foreign marketing authorization when designation is requested. Serious disease, unmet need, potential clinical advantage and benefit–risk must also satisfy SFDA.

The timing of that request therefore matters.

For the complete-data route, the guidance describes approximately 30 working days for designation review, 30 working days to submit the application after designation and a 60-working-day scientific assessment. Information requests affect elapsed time.

Crucially, the guidance permits access negotiations with healthcare entities to proceed alongside application review.

Regulatory assessment and preparation for delivery can move together.

Casgevy demonstrates that the program can accommodate an individualized cell therapy. Its Saudi approval on January 9, 2024 followed British approval by less than two months.

Its logistics are also relevant: collection at an authorized center, specialist manufacturing and return of the product for treatment.

𝗔 𝗦𝗔𝗨𝗗𝗜 𝗙𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥 𝗕𝗘𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗔𝗟.

SFDA’s special-access guideline recognizes three alternative eligibility conditions:

• Matching product registration by a listed reference regulator, including MHRA.

• Approval or permission from a reference regulator under the relevant access-program provision.

• A matching product application already under Saudi registration.

A Saudi filing can therefore satisfy an eligibility condition for a separately authorized access program.

Northwest’s existing UK compassionate-use service makes the second route worth clarifying directly with SFDA. The English text refers to permission for the program; the Arabic wording refers to the drug.

British approval would establish the reference-registration alternative while changing eligibility for a new Breakthrough request.

The strategic task is to select and sequence the available routes as regulatory status changes.

The October special-access guideline includes rare-disease requests, a seven-working-day response target and permissions lasting up to 12 months, renewable. Program and import permissions remain necessary.

The applicant funds the program and commits to free product for enrolled patients under the guideline’s conditions.

That makes funding part of the access plan from the outset. Someone must cover manufacture, logistics and care.

𝗢𝗡𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗦𝗨𝗣𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧 𝗬𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗦 𝗢𝗙 𝗧𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗧𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧.

DCVax-L requires suitable tumor material and immune cells.

Tumor material must be preserved under the appropriate manufacturing protocol. Routine formalin-fixed pathology material cannot simply substitute. Suitable previously banked material may sometimes be available.

The immune-cell starting material comes from leukapheresis.

NHS Blood and Transplant’s collaboration supports collection and specialist processing. Initial work involves Leeds and Oxford, with expansion being explored across a service operating apheresis units in ten English cities.

NHSBT’s announcement describes the intended scope as glioblastoma “as well as all solid tumours.”

That is a broad development ambition for the platform, with evidence and authorization required for particular uses.

The manufacturing model explains why collection capacity matters so much. Northwest reports approximately eight days of production plus release testing to produce a multi-year set of frozen doses.

A successful collection and manufacturing cycle can support repeated treatment. Each subsequent dose does not require another complete production cycle.

That separates three operational demands: collecting new patients, manufacturing their batches, and storing and administering the resulting doses.

It also supports centralized production with repeated international shipments.

The expense of manufacture is concentrated early. Payment timing is a contractual question; multi-year doses do not automatically mean prepaid revenue.

Saudi Arabia already has relevant infrastructure. King Faisal Specialist Hospital has treated more than 200 CAR-T patients and developed local production. Casgevy has an authorized Saudi treatment-center model.

Apheresis, patient identification, frozen-product handling and specialist administration are established capabilities in the Kingdom.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗘𝗖𝗞𝗣𝗢𝗜𝗡𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗘𝗡𝗗𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗣𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗨𝗡𝗜𝗧𝗬.

SPIMACO Bio’s Shilpa agreement covers PD-1 biosimilars. Shilpa’s disclosed development pipeline includes pembrolizumab and nivolumab, although the agreement announcement does not individually identify the licensed molecules.

Pembrolizumab is paired with dendritic-cell vaccination in UCLA’s recurrent-glioblastoma trial and a Pittsburgh ovarian-cancer study listing Northwest as a collaborator.

Northwest’s prospective Saudi partner is building capabilities relevant to both dendritic-cell vaccination and the checkpoint drugs used alongside it.

That provides a commercial and scientific basis for exploring a broader regional cancer-immunotherapy program around the initial DCVax-L collaboration.

𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗟𝗜𝗔𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗣𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗢𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗘𝗡𝗧’𝗦 𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧 𝗕𝗢𝗧𝗧𝗟𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗞.

Ruth Jones’s questions 41560 and 41561 seek national brain-tumor preservation standards, retention of suitable surplus tissue and consideration of preservation in the Chalmers review.

Answers are requested for November 17.

NHS England has completed a freezer-capacity gap analysis. Published answers have not supplied a funded rollout timetable or identified all sites receiving additional capacity.

The connection to vaccine access is direct: NHSBT supports the blood-derived input; preservation policy protects the tumor-derived input.

A treatment can become available after surgery. The opportunity to preserve the patient’s tissue may already have passed.

On November 4, Sharon Hodgson raised Braelyn’s case and access to DCVax-L in the Commons. The government committed to urgent examination by the Health Secretary.

The October 14 brain-cancer initiative promised the Chalmers review, a subsequent national action plan and a national clinical lead.

This gives Parliament identifiable implementation questions to pursue: preservation standards, funded infrastructure and responsibility for getting patients through the process.

𝗟𝗔𝗪𝗥𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘 𝗧𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗦 𝗥𝗘𝗚𝗨𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗪𝗜𝗧𝗛 𝗗𝗘𝗟𝗜𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗬.

Tallon is MHRA’s chief executive and chairs its highest executive decision-making body.

Previously, he was deputy chief executive at Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust, overseeing strategy, technology and innovation. His experience includes running healthcare services as well as leading their regulator.

His Saudi relationship predates this summit. SFDA documented a bilateral meeting between Tallon and Aljadhey in October 2025 concerning regulatory cooperation and medicine quality, safety and efficacy.

The new memorandum develops an established relationship.

Tallon has now signed the Saudi agreement and is co-chairing the summit session where Dr. Annalisa Jenkins will deliver a keynote and join the panel.

Northwest appointed Jenkins in April to support its dendritic-cell platform, regulatory strategy and commercialization, explicitly including broader solid tumors and rare cancers.

Her responsibilities overlap closely with the summit’s discussion of investment, policy and international delivery. The programme lists her under The Conscience Collective and Genomics England.

This is a substantive institutional connection. It does not establish a private DCVax decision.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗪𝗔𝗧𝗖𝗛.

November 17 begins with the summit’s advanced-therapy and rare-disease session, involving MHRA, NICE, patient advocates and investors.

The international-regulation session includes Aljadhey and MHRA’s James Pound. The closing plenary begins at 15:15 London time, 10:15 a.m. Eastern, with Tallon co-chairing and Jenkins speaking.

The programme also includes an MHRA parliamentary reception and closing commitments involving the science minister.

The summit is already being used for announcements: the Saudi MOU and MHRA’s Women’s Health Programme. Tallon’s opening recap emphasized faster trials, recruitment and translating science into patient benefit.

Also on November 17 are the requested tissue-preservation answers and a Westminster Hall debate on MHRA performance. Its advertised scope concerns safety, transparency and accountability.

On November 18, Siobhain McDonagh has a PMQs slot. Her supplementary topic has not been published.

The Chalmers review was asked to report within three months of the October 14 announcement. That points to mid-January 2027, approximately January 14 by calendar arithmetic. A separate exact publication date has not been announced. The national action plan follows.

These are opportunities for specific commitments, rather than dates assigned to a DCVax approval.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗖𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗢 𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗨𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗢𝗕𝗟𝗜𝗚𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦.

Northwest’s November 13 filing still describes negotiations toward a definitive Saudi agreement and continued engagement in the British review. A Saudi DCVax filing has not been publicly verified.

The next agreement becomes consequential through its terms.

Development funding, technology-transfer payments, purchase commitments or funded access arrangements could change how much expansion Northwest must finance from its own balance sheet.

Those commitments have not been disclosed for Northwest. They are what investors should examine when a definitive agreement appears.

The financial stakes are substantial. Northwest reported $725,000 in cash at September 30 and significant current liabilities, while also disclosing a subsequent October financing agreement.

SPIMACO’s resources become useful to Northwest through enforceable obligations: who pays, when payment occurs, who performs the work and what happens if milestones are missed.

An agreement assigning those responsibilities could strengthen Northwest in three ways:

• Share the cost of expansion.

• Put regional execution in the hands of an experienced partner.

• Create income opportunities from existing production, technology and expertise.

That is a more consequential development than another statement of intent.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗣𝗦 𝗖𝗔𝗡 𝗕𝗘 𝗠𝗘𝗔𝗦𝗨𝗥𝗘𝗗.

The milestones are a definitive agreement, an appropriate SFDA designation or filing, an authorized access route, named treatment centers and the manufacturing and import arrangements required to deliver doses.

The work can overlap. Regulatory review, access negotiations and preparation of treatment centers can proceed alongside one another where the applicable rules permit.

The regional opportunity also extends beyond Saudi Arabia. Northwest’s MOU allows additional Gulf territories by agreement. SFDA became the first full ICMRA member from the Middle East and North Africa in 2025, and its cooperation with Bahrain includes a 2024 regulatory agreement.

Each jurisdiction retains its own requirements, but Northwest would not be developing regional relationships from nothing.

𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗔𝗡𝗡𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗖𝗘𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗦 𝗧𝗢 𝗔𝗖𝗖𝗘𝗦𝗦.

NHSBT helps organize the route into manufacturing. Northwest brings the technology and production. SPIMACO offers a prospective route into another healthcare system. The MHRA–SFDA agreement gives the regulators a framework for working together.

Each addresses a different part of the same problem: making a personalized treatment deliverable across borders.

The opportunity is to use existing production, retain the value of the intellectual property and develop local manufacturing in stages, with a partner carrying defined responsibilities.

For patients, preparation cannot wait for every institutional decision.

A regulator can authorize treatment later. A company can expand a factory later. Neither can recover a patient’s discarded tumor.

The route begins with suitable tissue and ends with a released dose in a treating physician’s hands.

The decisive next announcement would identify who funds that route, who supplies the vaccine and where patients can receive it. That is the agreement that would turn Northwest’s Saudi opportunity into an operating business.
